```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(gt)
library(e1071)
library(tmap)

#course data (read once for the whole page)
rurality <- st_read("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jucardwell/geog391/main/data/nc_tracts_rurality.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
climate_normals <- st_read("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jucardwell/geog391/main/data/climate_normals.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
county_acs <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1hXVtKL_33c4QRw6_Z9LlYqjgisdYCRqX", quiet = TRUE)
tract_acs <- st_read("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jucardwell/geog391/main/data/nc_tract_acs_2023.geojson", quiet = TRUE)

#numbers quoted in the text below come from here, so they stay right if the data changes
fmt <- function(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
n_tracts <- nrow(rurality)
n_normals <- nrow(climate_normals)
ruca_mode <- rurality |> st_drop_geometry() |> count(ruca_code) |> slice_max(n, n = 1)
```

## Part 1: Walkthrough {#walkthrough}

Run each chunk in your own .Rmd. You will reuse this code in Part 2.

### Step 1: Load the Data

::: {.why}
We'll use rurality codes (RUCA) for `r fmt(n_tracts, 0)` North Carolina census tracts from the [USDA Economic Research Service](https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/rural-urban-commuting-area-codes), and 1991 to 2020 summer temperature normals at `r fmt(n_normals, 0)` locations across the U.S. from [NOAA](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cdo-web/). Both are already summaries: the normals are 30-year averages, so anything we calculate from them describes data that has already been averaged once.
:::

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(gt)
library(e1071)
library(tmap)

#rurality (RUCA codes) for NC census tracts
rurality <- st_read("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jucardwell/geog391/main/data/nc_tracts_rurality.geojson")

#summer temperature normals, 1991-2020
climate_normals <- st_read("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jucardwell/geog391/main/data/climate_normals.geojson")
```

### Step 2: Describe a Categorical Variable

::: {.why}
`ruca_code` is nominal, so the only descriptive statistics that make sense are counts and the mode. A bar chart shows the counts.
:::

```{r}
#count tracts in each RUCA category
ruca_counts <- rurality |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(ruca_code) |>
  summarise(n = n())

ruca_counts |> gt()

#bar chart (coord_flip puts the long labels on the side)
ggplot(ruca_counts, aes(x = ruca_code, y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "RUCA code", y = "Number of census tracts")
```

The mode is **`r ruca_mode$ruca_code`**, with `r fmt(ruca_mode$n, 0)` tracts.

### Step 3: Map It

```{r}
#map the raw tract data, not the counts
tm_shape(rurality) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "ruca_code", fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = "paired"))
```

### Step 4: Describe a Numeric Variable

::: {.why}
For an interval or ratio variable, describe the center (mean, median), the spread (standard deviation, range) and the shape (skewness). Always count the missing values first.
:::

```{r}
#descriptive statistics for summer temperature
climate_normals |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    num_na = sum(is.na(summer_temp)),
    mean = mean(summer_temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(summer_temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(summer_temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    min = min(summer_temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(summer_temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    skewness = skewness(summer_temp, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Statistic", values_to = "Value") |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = Value, decimals = 2)
```

### Step 5: Plot the Distribution

::: {.why}
A histogram shows the shape of the distribution. A boxplot shows the median, the quartiles and any outliers.
:::

```{r}
#histogram
ggplot(climate_normals, aes(x = summer_temp)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Summer temperature (°F)", y = "Count")

#boxplot
ggplot(climate_normals, aes(y = summer_temp)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightgrey") +
  labs(y = "Summer temperature (°F)")
```

## Part 2: Partner Practice {#partner-practice}

Both partners describe `pct_no_veh`, the percent of households without a vehicle, from the 2019 to 2023 [American Community Survey](https://data.census.gov/). Partner A uses North Carolina's 100 counties and Partner B uses its census tracts. Each task tells you in parentheses which walkthrough step to reuse.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#Partner A: NC counties
county_acs <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1hXVtKL_33c4QRw6_Z9LlYqjgisdYCRqX")

#Partner B: NC census tracts
tract_acs <- st_read("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jucardwell/geog391/main/data/nc_tract_acs_2023.geojson")
```

:::: {.partners}
::: {.partner .partner-a}
### Partner A: Counties

1. Make a descriptive statistics table for `pct_no_veh`. *(Step 4)*
2. Plot a histogram and a boxplot. *(Step 5)*
3. Map `pct_no_veh` by county. *(Step 3)*
4. Find the county with the highest value. Use `slice_max()`, and keep `county_name`.

When you finish, bring the mean, median, standard deviation and maximum to Part 3, along with the county that has the maximum.
:::

::: {.partner .partner-b}
### Partner B: Census Tracts

1. Make a descriptive statistics table for `pct_no_veh`. Count the missing values. *(Step 4)*
2. Plot a histogram and a boxplot. *(Step 5)*
3. Map `pct_no_veh` by tract. *(Step 3)*
4. Find the tract with the highest value. Its `GEOID` starts with the state and county codes, so you can tell which county it is in.

When you finish, bring the mean, median, standard deviation and maximum to Part 3, along with the tract that has the maximum.
:::
::::

## Part 3: Together {#together}

1. Fill in the table with both sets of numbers.
2. Explain to each other why the tract numbers are so much more spread out than the county numbers.
3. A regional transit agency wants to know where households without cars are concentrated so it can plan a new bus route. Decide together which scale it should use, and why.

| Scale | Mean | Median | Standard deviation | Maximum |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Counties (Partner A) | | | | |
| Census tracts (Partner B) | | | | |

::: {.deliver}
Each pair turns in one index card before leaving. Write both of your names on it, fill in the eight numbers from the table, and add two or three sentences saying which scale the transit agency should use and why.
:::

## Answer Key {#answer-key .answer-key}

```{r key-values, include = FALSE}
describe <- function(d) {
  d |>
    st_drop_geometry() |>
    summarise(n = n(), num_na = sum(is.na(pct_no_veh)),
              mean = mean(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE), median = median(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE),
              sd = sd(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE), min = min(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE),
              max = max(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE), skewness = skewness(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE))
}
a <- describe(county_acs)
b <- describe(tract_acs)
a_top <- county_acs |> st_drop_geometry() |> slice_max(pct_no_veh, n = 1)
b_top <- tract_acs |> st_drop_geometry() |> slice_max(pct_no_veh, n = 1)
```

| Item | Counties (A) | Tracts (B) |
|---|---|---|
| Number of units | `r a$n` | `r fmt(b$n, 0)` (`r b$num_na` missing) |
| Mean | `r fmt(a$mean)` | `r fmt(b$mean)` |
| Median | `r fmt(a$median)` | `r fmt(b$median)` |
| Standard deviation | `r fmt(a$sd)` | `r fmt(b$sd)` |
| Minimum to maximum | `r fmt(a$min)` to `r fmt(a$max)` | `r fmt(b$min)` to `r fmt(b$max)` |
| Skewness | `r fmt(a$skewness, 2)` | `r fmt(b$skewness, 2)` |
| Highest | `r a_top$county_name` | tract `r b_top$GEOID[1]` |

A good card says something like this. The means are almost the same, but the tracts are far more spread out, with a standard deviation of `r fmt(b$sd)` against `r fmt(a$sd)` for counties. Each county averages together tracts with very different shares, so the high and low tracts cancel out. The tract distribution is also strongly right-skewed (skewness `r fmt(b$skewness, 2)`), which is why its mean sits well above its median. A tract that reports `r fmt(b$max, 0)`% is worth checking before you trust it, because estimates for small areas can be extreme. The transit agency should use tracts, because a bus route serves neighborhoods, and county averages hide the pockets it is looking for.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#### Partner A: counties ####
county_acs <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1hXVtKL_33c4QRw6_Z9LlYqjgisdYCRqX")

#A1: descriptive statistics (Step 4)
county_acs |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    num_na = sum(is.na(pct_no_veh)),
    mean = mean(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE),
    min = min(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE),
    skewness = skewness(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Statistic", values_to = "Value") |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = Value, decimals = 2)

#A2: histogram and boxplot (Step 5)
ggplot(county_acs, aes(x = pct_no_veh)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Households without a vehicle (%)", y = "Number of counties")

ggplot(county_acs, aes(y = pct_no_veh)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightgrey") +
  labs(y = "Households without a vehicle (%)")

#A3: map (Step 3)
tm_shape(county_acs) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "pct_no_veh")

#A4: county with the highest value
county_acs |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  slice_max(pct_no_veh, n = 1) |>
  select(county_name, pct_no_veh)

#### Partner B: census tracts ####
tract_acs <- st_read("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jucardwell/geog391/main/data/nc_tract_acs_2023.geojson")

#B1: descriptive statistics, including missing values (Step 4)
tract_acs |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    num_na = sum(is.na(pct_no_veh)),
    mean = mean(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE),
    min = min(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE),
    skewness = skewness(pct_no_veh, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Statistic", values_to = "Value") |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = Value, decimals = 2)

#B2: histogram and boxplot (Step 5)
ggplot(tract_acs, aes(x = pct_no_veh)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Households without a vehicle (%)", y = "Number of tracts")

ggplot(tract_acs, aes(y = pct_no_veh)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightgrey") +
  labs(y = "Households without a vehicle (%)")

#B3: map (Step 3)
tm_shape(tract_acs) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "pct_no_veh")

#B4: tract with the highest value (37 = NC, the next three digits are the county)
tract_acs |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  slice_max(pct_no_veh, n = 1) |>
  select(GEOID, pct_no_veh)
```
